meta.subline: 13 JUL 2026 · 12:00 GST · US ROUND-4: 140 TARGETS, FIRST SEA-DRONE STRIKES · IRAN HITS 3+ GCC STATES · MUSCAT TALKS COLLAPSE · STRAIT OPEN/CLOSED DISPUTED · BRENT ~$79

banner.html: US LAUNCHES A FOURTH STRIKE ROUND — 140 TARGETS, FIRST-EVER SEA-DRONE STRIKES. Iran retaliates against GCC bases · Muscat talks collapse with nothing agreed — Iran accuses US of pressuring Oman · Strait status now openly disputed: Trump says ‘open,’ Iran says passage ‘not possible’

wire.src: CENTCOM · The Hill · CBS · Al Jazeera
wire.title: US Round 4 — CENTCOM says it struck 140 Iranian military targets, using one-way attack sea drones for the first time alongside aircraft, warships and aerial drones.
wire.full: CENTCOM said Trump ordered the strikes to ‘hold Iranian forces accountable’ and degrade Iran’s ability to attack commercial shipping. Targets: air-defence systems, coastal radar sites, missile and drone capabilities, and small boats. The debut of one-way attack unmanned surface vessels (USVs) is the notable new capability — previously only aerial drones and manned platforms were used. Reporting on scale varies: CENTCOM/The Hill cite 140 targets; CNBC and Al Jazeera frame it as ‘dozens’ of additional targets in a fourth wave.
wire.why: Two firsts in one strike package. Hitting coastal radar and air-defence (not just boats and ports) means the US is now dismantling the sensor-and-shooter network Iran needs to enforce closure — a shift from punishing attacks to disabling the capability itself. The sea-drone debut signals the US intends to contest the water directly, cheaply and without risking crews.

wire.title: Iran retaliates against US bases across the GCC — Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan confirmed; some reporting adds Qatar and Oman.
wire.full: The IRGC said it struck US-linked military sites in response to Round 4. Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan are named consistently across sources; broader lists (ms.now, some CNBC copy) add Qatar and — most consequentially — Oman, the very state mediating the talks. Whether Oman was targeted is decomposed in VERIFY. No confirmed casualties reported; Gulf air defences claim interceptions.
wire.why: If Oman was genuinely struck, Iran hit its own mediator on the same weekend the mediation collapsed — either a loss of control or a message that no US-hosting state is exempt, mediator or not. That single disputed fact changes how to read the diplomatic track entirely, which is why it belongs in VERIFY rather than the headline.

wire.title: Muscat talks collapse with nothing agreed — Iran accuses the US of ‘overt and covert pressure’ on Oman that blocked a Hormuz-management deal.
wire.full: Saturday’s Araghchi–Albusaidi talks in Muscat ‘wrapped with little decided.’ Iran publicly blamed US pressure on Oman for preventing agreement on arrangements to manage the strait and its traffic routes. Trump separately says talks will continue under the Vance/Rubio/Witkoff/Kushner team — but confirms the June ceasefire is ‘scrapped.’ The two-corridor formula that was on the table 11 Jul did not close.
wire.why: This is the load-bearing failure of the day. The base-case scenario from 12 Jul — Muscat produces a pause — is now failing in real time: the talks that were supposed to be the off-ramp produced nothing, and each side is blaming the other in public. The parallel-tracks pattern is under stress: the diplomatic track didn’t just stall, it broke while the kinetic track accelerated to Round 4.

wire.src: LSEG · Al Jazeera · The National · Goldman
wire.title: Brent jumps to ~$79 (+3.9–4.1%), reversing the retreat toward pre-war levels; just 6 vessels tracked crossing Hormuz in a 12-hour window.
wire.full: Brent traded around $78.96–$79.16 by 09:01 GST, up ~4% on the day and building on +5.4% last week; WTI near $74. LSEG/tanker tracking recorded only six vessels crossing the strait between 18:00 GMT Thu and 06:00 GMT Fri, versus 18–22 daily crossings earlier this month. Goldman: ‘a serious re-escalation could reintensify the short-run upside risk to oil prices.’
wire.why: The market has stopped treating the closure as pure posture. A ~4% jump on top of last week’s 5.4% — with transit collapsing to single digits — is traders pricing real supply risk, not a negotiating bluff. For a UAE resident this is the first day the price signal and the physical signal (6 ships) point the same way: the disruption is real, not rhetorical.

wire.title: Strait status openly disputed — Trump and CENTCOM insist the waterway is ‘open’; Iran’s strait authority says passage is ‘not possible.’
wire.full: The US position: Iran ‘does not control’ Hormuz and it remains open to traffic. Iran’s position: following the closure declaration and Round-4 exchange, passage is ‘not possible.’ The physical evidence sits between the two claims — six transits in twelve hours is neither a normal open strait (~18–22/day) nor a hard zero. Both governments are asserting the reading that suits them.
wire.why: The open-vs-closed dispute is now the informational battleground, and the honest answer is neither label. ‘Open’ and ‘not possible’ are both political claims; the operational truth is a strait that is transitable only by those willing to run a gauntlet, which is why traffic is down ~70% but not zero. Watch transit counts, not adjectives.

wire.title: Context — the trigger for this cycle: IRGC hit M/V GFS Galaxy 9nm off Oman, one crew missing, then declared the strait closed ‘until further notice.’
wire.full: The Cyprus-flagged container ship was disabled by engine-room fire; a civilian crew member remains missing. CENTCOM called it a ‘blatant attack’; the IRGC called it a ‘warning shot’ at a vessel on an ‘unapproved route.’ The closure declaration and the three prior strike rounds (7–12 Jul) set up today’s Round 4.
wire.why: Kept on the wire as the causal anchor: every event today traces back to this single incident 48 hours ago. The missing mariner remains unresolved — still the most likely trip-wire for a further hardening if confirmed dead.

wire.src: Ynet · Times of Israel · Fox — Israeli officials; no T2 confirmation
wire.title: Still open: Israel ‘poised’ to rejoin strikes — no fresh T2 confirmation of force movement as of today.
wire.full: The 11 Jul Israeli-official readiness signals have not been followed, as of this update, by any T2-confirmed strike package or force movement. Israel remains outside the MOU and has not accepted the Lebanon-withdrawal linkage. This item is carried forward, unchanged in status, precisely because its resolution would be the single highest-consequence development.
wire.why: Deliberately held at PENDING for a second day. The value is in what has NOT happened: through a fourth US strike round and a diplomatic collapse, Israel has still not visibly re-entered. Each day of non-entry modestly lowers the tail scenario — but a single T2 confirmation would reverse that instantly.

status.v: US Round 4 in six days: CENTCOM reports 140 targets and the first-ever use of one-way attack sea drones, hitting air-defence, coastal radar, missile/drone sites and small boats. The campaign has shifted from punishing attacks to dismantling Iran’s enforcement capability.
IRGC struck US bases across the GCC — Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan confirmed; Qatar and Oman reported by some sources (disputed). No confirmed casualties; Gulf air defences claim interceptions.

COLLAPSED for now. Muscat talks ended with nothing agreed; Iran accuses the US of pressuring Oman. Trump says talks continue under the Vance team but confirms the June ceasefire is ‘scrapped.’ The two-corridor formula did not close.
Disputed open/closed: US says open, Iran says passage ‘not possible.’ Physical reality between the two — 6 transits in 12h vs ~18–22/day. Brent ~$79 (+4%).

verify.who: Was Oman — the mediator — actually struck by Iran?
verify.quote: Iran’s strikes targeted American military bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan, Oman and Qatar. — broader source list

rows.c: Iran struck US bases in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan.
rows.n: These three appear consistently across CBS, CNBC and Al Jazeera reporting of the IRGC statement — the reliable core of the retaliation.

rows.c: Whether Qatar and Oman were also targeted.
rows.n: Broader source lists (ms.now, some CNBC copy) add Qatar and Oman; the narrower, more-cited lists do not. Oman being hit while hosting the talks is extraordinary if true — hence held as disputed until a Gulf-state official source (QNA, Oman MoD) confirms or denies.
No confirmed casualties reported on either side of the exchange; Gulf air defences claim interceptions. No independent battle-damage assessment yet.

verify.who: Is the Strait of Hormuz open or closed?
verify.handle: Trump/CENTCOM vs Iran strait authority · 13 Jul
verify.reach: US officials · Iran strait authority · LSEG
verify.quote: The US says the strait is open and Iran ‘does not control’ it; Iran’s strait authority says passage is ‘not possible.’

rows.n: Both are political assertions. Do not adopt either as fact — render the conflict. The US needs it to be ‘open’ to deny Iran leverage; Iran needs it ‘closed’ to assert control.
rows.src: irreconcilable by design — US vs Iran

rows.c: Traffic has collapsed to roughly 6 transits in 12 hours.
rows.n: LSEG/tanker tracking: six crossings in a twelve-hour window vs ~18–22/day earlier this month — a ~70% drop. This is the measurable ground truth beneath the dueling adjectives.

rows.c: ‘Open’ is technically truer than ‘closed’ — but misleading.
rows.n: Ships CAN transit (six did) so it is not a hard closure; but at ~70% below normal and under fire, it is not a functioning open strait either. The honest reading is ‘transitable under threat,’ which neither government will say.
rows.src: PARTIAL · physical data splits the difference

verify.who: Did the US really use sea drones for the first time?
verify.quote: American forces struck using fighter aircraft, naval vessels, one-way attack aerial drones and one-way attack sea drones for the first time.

rows.c: The first-use claim is carried by multiple outlets attributing it to CENTCOM.
rows.n: CNBC and Al Jazeera both report the sea-drone (USV) debut, sourced to CENTCOM’s own account of the strike package.

rows.c: Independent confirmation of USV use and effect.
rows.n: As with the target count, this rests on CENTCOM’s account; no independent OSINT imagery or battle-damage assessment has corroborated the sea-drone strikes specifically yet.

market.txt: Brent ~$78.96–$79.16 by 09:01 GST, up ~4% on the day and building on +5.4% last week; WTI near $74. Only 6 vessels crossed Hormuz in a 12-hour window (vs ~18–22/day). Goldman warns a serious re-escalation could reintensify short-run upside risk to prices. The market and the physical transit signal are now pointing the same way for the first time this cycle — both saying real disruption, not posture.

scenarios.lab: Contested-strait stalemate — strikes continue, talks limp on, no clean resolution
scenarios.p: Now the modal outcome. Round 4 degraded Iran’s enforcement kit but did not stop it; the Muscat channel produced nothing but continues on life support under the Vance team. The strait stays ‘transitable under threat’ — neither reopened nor hard-closed — with periodic strike rounds and retaliation salvos. This is escalation without resolution, and the trajectory of the last 48 hours points here. Analytical judgment, not sourced fact.

scenarios.lab: Off-ramp reopens — a face-saving Hormuz-management deal within days
scenarios.p: The parallel-tracks pattern reasserts: both sides keep the Vance team engaged, and the two-corridor formula (permits yes, tolls no) is revived with new wording on the disputed Article 5. Downgraded from 40% because the base case’s core mechanism — Muscat producing a pause — just visibly failed, and each side is now blaming the other in public, which raises the cost of climbing down.

scenarios.lab: Rupture — Israel re-enters and/or a mass-casualty event ends the deal outright
scenarios.p: A confirmed mariner death on the GFS Galaxy, a lethal hit on a GCC base, or a T2-confirmed Israeli strike package converts the crisis into an unrecoverable war. Held at 25%: through four US strike rounds and a diplomatic collapse, none of these trip-wires has yet been crossed — but the collapse of the talks removes the strongest brake that was holding this scenario down.

uae_means: Day 136 is the first day the numbers and the ships agree: Brent up ~4% to ~$79 AND only six vessels crossing the strait in twelve hours — the disruption is now real, not rhetorical, and import and fuel costs will feel it. Yet the personal-safety picture for a UAE resident is still steadier than the headlines: through four US strike rounds Iran has hit Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan (Qatar and Oman disputed) and — for a sixth straight day — has NOT struck the UAE, the war’s most-targeted state pre-MOU. Airspace remains open; flights are running. The two things that changed today and matter locally: (1) the diplomatic off-ramp visibly failed at Muscat, so the ‘this de-escalates within days’ base case is weaker than it was 24 hours ago — plan for a contested strait for weeks, not days; and (2) the strait is now a genuine combat zone with US sea drones in the water, so shipping-dependent costs (fuel, imports, war-risk insurance) resume climbing. Watch three things: UAE MOD/WAM language for any shift toward self-defence, whether Oman was actually struck (it would mean even mediators aren’t exempt), and the Vance team’s movements — their re-engagement is the clearest signal the off-ramp isn’t dead. Severe and worsening, still contained — but the brake that was diplomacy just slipped.

triggers.t: Confirmation on whether Oman was struck — a Gulf-state source (QNA, Oman MoD) resolving the disputed target list. If yes, mediators are no longer exempt and the diplomatic track is in deeper trouble than it looks.
The Vance team’s next move — re-engagement (new venue, new draft) is the clearest de-escalation signal; a public walk-away is the counter-signal that the risk scenario is locking in.
Any T2-confirmed Israeli force movement — still the single highest-consequence trigger. Six days of non-entry; one confirmation flips the tail scenario to base.
A confirmed fatality — GFS Galaxy mariner or a GCC base — the first death of this cycle would harden every Western position and could end the deal outright.

Transit count, not adjectives — if crossings fall toward zero, ‘not possible’ becomes true; if they climb back toward ~18/day, ‘open’ wins. The number settles the open/closed dispute that words cannot.

hist: War began 28 Feb 2026 — Ali Khamenei killed; Mojtaba Khamenei became Supreme Leader; Iran fired 1,800+ projectiles at the UAE alone (13 killed, 224 injured). MOU signed 17 Jun (the ‘Islamabad Memorandum’): 14 points, 60-day toll-free Hormuz, $300bn reconstruction. Peak of 70 crossings 24 Jun. 4–6 Jul: Ali Khamenei’s state funeral — crowds called for Trump’s death. 7 Jul: two tankers struck, a third within 24h; US hit ~90 targets, re-imposed oil sanctions. 8–9 Jul: two strike nights (14 killed, 78 wounded); Iran hit four Gulf states; Trump declared the ceasefire ‘over.’ 10 Jul: southern-lane traffic collapsed. 11 Jul: IRGC hit the GFS Galaxy and declared the strait CLOSED; US Round 3 followed; Trump and Mojtaba traded personal threats; the Muscat channel opened. 12 Jul: the two-corridor formula was on the table. 13 Jul (Day 136): US Round 4 — 140 targets and the first-ever sea-drone strikes; Iran retaliated across the GCC; the Muscat talks collapsed with nothing agreed; the strait’s status split into a US-‘open’ / Iran-‘not possible’ dispute; Brent hit ~$79 as transit fell to 6 ships in 12 hours. The off-ramp that opened two days ago has, for now, closed.
